$schema_note: issue #55's per-feature truth-source labeling. `source` is one of postgres|invariant|none, per TRUTH_MODEL.md. A `none`-labeled feature must never enter a scored pack (#53) until it gains either a postgres or invariant source - see TRUTH_MODEL.md's 'Enforcement' section.

features.note: tinytable's grammar is a subset of standard SQL - oracle.py's postgres backend adjudicates every statement/query it can produce.
PostgreSQL adjudicates the underlying type system; tinytable's own exact-match strictness is a documented intentional divergence (oracle.py's INTENTIONAL_DIVERGENCES), not left unlabeled.

standard SQL three-valued logic - PostgreSQL is a faithful independent implementation. (This is the class of bug that shipped in clean/tinytable's own Not predicate until issue #55's rollout caught it - see git history around this file's introduction.)

arithmetic/concat/NULL-propagation are standard SQL; tinytable's exact operand typing is a documented intentional divergence, same as Column Types above. One sub-rule is a documented exception within this otherwise-postgres-adjudicable section: 'division by zero is NULL' (verified empirically that real PostgreSQL instead raises - oracle.py's QUERY_DIVERGENCES) means the postgres backend can never adjudicate the expr-division-by-zero-returns-zero mutant either way; that one operator's ground truth is SPEC.md/the official suite alone. Also confirmed empirically (see mutate.py's expr-arithmetic-bool-not-excluded): the sqlite backend alone would miss that specific defect (sqlite has no real BOOLEAN type, so it silently agrees with the mutant) - the postgres backend catches it, real evidence for why #56 added it.
standard SQL, including NULL placement - PostgreSQL adjudicates directly.
standard SQL - PostgreSQL has no bare-OFFSET restriction either, unlike sqlite3 (see oracle.py's _to_sqlite_sql).
an index is a pure optimization: the invariant is 'same result as an unindexed query', which oracle.py's result comparison verifies without needing any PostgreSQL-specific index concept at all.
standard SQL UNIQUE semantics including NULL exemption - PostgreSQL adjudicates directly.

features.spec_section: Constraints: NOT NULL / CHECK / FOREIGN KEY
features.note: standard SQL; CHECK's three-valued semantics and FOREIGN KEY's RESTRICT-only behavior both verified empirically to match real PostgreSQL (see oracle.py's module docstring).

standard SQL savepoint semantics. Known gap (documented, not silent): oracle.py's blind-spot fix does not yet extend to a tinytable REJECTION of one of these four control statements specifically - see oracle.py's module docstring.
standard SQL aggregate semantics, including COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col) NULL handling.

features.spec_section: Grammar v2: session / step / permutation (ordering only, single-threaded)
features.note: each step's own SQL is ordinary PG-adjudicable statement/query content.

features.spec_section: Grammar v2: session / step / permutation (cross-session interleaving/visibility)
features.note: no MVCC visibility semantics exist yet (see #10); admissibility.py's conflict-serializability checker (#21, run_sql_tests.py --check-admissibility) is the local invariant this repo already has for it, per #22's 'history-admissibility, not a reference model' policy.

SPEC.md is explicit: 'nothing wires Database to this Simulation yet ... none of this has an SQL-visible effect' - not scorable today. #22's planned invariant once #11's WAL lands: committed data survives restart, uncommitted data never becomes visible, recovery is idempotent - none of that is a per-feature reference model.

advance_clock has no SQL-visible effect yet (no TTL/retention feature reads the clock); threshold is grammar-only, not yet executing (#21's history-across-repeat-iterations plumbing isn't implemented). repeat itself is just a loop around already-classified statement/query records.
no query planner exists yet (#12) - reported skipped, not scorable.
Database.stats() internal counters (#21) are inherently not SQL-visible/PG-adjudicable - bounded/converges are exactly the kind of local invariant #22 describes as the right lightweight tool here.
